title: FP8/INT8 quant sanity evals — notes + drift thresholds (Applied ML)
content:
Context
- This is the Applied ML “sanity evals” scratchpad for the FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint.
- Goal: catch obvious quality/correctness regressions early (and cheaply), and provide practical drift thresholds + “watchlist prompts” to run during perf work.
- Not trying to be a full model quality evaluation. This is a guardrail to avoid shipping something that breaks customer workloads.

What we mean by “sanity” here
1) Numerical drift checks (token-level + logprob-ish proxies where available)
2) Output behavior checks (format adherence, tool/function call JSON validity, refusal patterns)
3) Lightweight semantic checks on a small prompt set (heuristic scoring + a few golden answers)

Primary comparisons
- Baseline: FP16 (current shipped runtime build for the same model version)
- Candidates:
  - FP8 (attention + GEMM paths depending on model/kernel availability)
  - INT8 (GEMM-heavy path; attention may remain higher precision depending on op coverage)
- We should always compare within the same decoding parameters (temp/top_p/top_k, repetition penalty, max_new_tokens) and same seed where supported.

Suggested drift thresholds (practical, not academic)
Note: thresholds below assume deterministic-ish settings (temperature 0 or low, fixed seed if supported, no sampling when doing strict drift checks). For “realistic sampling” we loosen acceptance and focus on distribution/format.

A) Deterministic drift (temp=0, top_p=1, max_new_tokens fixed)
- Token agreement (exact match) over the full generated span:
  - Green: >= 98% identical tokens (per prompt, averaged over prompt set)
  - Yellow: 95–98% (allowed only if no behavior regressions; require manual spot check on sensitive categories)
  - Red: < 95% (block for shipping / block perf-canary promotion)
- First divergence index (where first token differs):
  - Green: median divergence >= 64 tokens
  - Yellow: median divergence 32–64 tokens
  - Red: median divergence < 32 tokens
Rationale: kernel changes that alter early decoding tokens tend to be user-visible and correlate with “it feels different” feedback.

B) Structured output / formatting
Run a small set of “format forcing” prompts (see watchlist below).
- JSON validity / schema validity (where schema known):
  - Green: >= 99% valid
  - Yellow: 97–99% (allowed only for internal experiments; not for default)
  - Red: < 97%
- Tool call arguments parseable (same as above; treat parse failures as hard failures)

C) Safety / refusal patterns (very small set)
We do NOT attempt broad policy eval here, but we do want to catch obvious refusal flips.
- For prompts expected to refuse: refusal rate should not drop materially.
- For benign prompts: refusal rate should not spike.
Threshold (rough): no more than +/- 2 prompts change category on the small set. Anything larger needs investigation.

D) “Realistic” sampling drift (temp=0.7, top_p=0.95)
This is a canary for weird mode collapse / repetition / incoherence.
- Use heuristic flags:
  - repetition ratio (unique 3-grams / total 3-grams) should not drop > 5% vs FP16
  - average output length should not change > 10% for length-constrained prompts
- Manual spot check required if any heuristic triggers.

Prompt categories to watch closely (empirically sensitive to quant)
These are the ones that have historically shown differences when we change numeric paths, especially on long-context or high-perplexity spans.

1) Long-context retrieval / “needle” questions
- User provides long doc, asks for one specific detail.
- Failure mode: model becomes more “guessy” / confabulates, or misses the needle.
- Quant sensitivity: attention stability + KV cache interaction + scaling.

2) Multi-step arithmetic / chain-of-thought-like reasoning (without requiring CoT output)
- Prompts that require stable intermediate reasoning even if we only grade final.
- Failure mode: early token divergence changes the whole path.
- For sanity: we grade final numeric answer only (and sometimes intermediate if explicitly requested by prompt).

3) Code generation / syntax constraints
- Particularly bracket/indentation heavy code (Python, JSON, SQL).
- Failure mode: minor drift can break syntax; INT8 dequant/fusion issues can show up as more syntax errors.
- Use: compile/parse checks where possible.

4) Strict JSON / function calling
- “Return ONLY JSON, no trailing text” class.
- Failure mode: extra commentary text, missing quotes, NaNs, unescaped newlines.

5) Multilingual + transliteration
- Non-English (esp. CJK) prompts with strict formatting.
- Failure mode: subtle tokenization differences amplify; output can include garbled characters or mixed scripts.

6) Safety boundary prompts
- A few edge prompts to catch “refuse vs comply” flips.
- We keep this small and internal.

7) Summarization with citations / quotes
- Summaries that require quoting exact substrings from context.
- Failure mode: quote drift or hallucinated citations.

Proposed prompt set composition (small / fast)
Target: ~120 prompts total, runnable in < 20 minutes per model on a single GPU for temp=0 and ~30–40 minutes with sampling runs.
- 25 long-context retrieval
- 20 code/syntax
- 20 JSON/function calling / schema
- 15 multilingual
- 15 summarization with quotes
- 15 math/logic
- 10 safety boundary (internal)

Scoring / checks (cheap)
- Exact match for deterministic runs (token and text)
- JSON parse checks + schema validation (where we have schemas)
- Language-specific parsers (python ast, sql parse via lightweight lib if available)
- Simple “needle” regex checks for retrieval prompts (did it extract the exact value)
- Heuristic repetition / length checks for sampling

Operational notes (how we actually run during the sprint)
- For kernel bring-up: run deterministic set first. If it fails, don’t bother with sampling.
- Always pin:
  - model version / weights
  - runtime commit
  - quant mode (FP8 e4m3/e5m2 as per ADR; accumulation type)
  - decoding params
  - prompt set version
- Report:
  - pass/fail + top failures (prompt ids)
  - token agreement histogram
  - first divergence distribution
  - JSON validity rate

Triage checklist when drift is high
- Confirm determinism: same seed, same decoding config, same tokenizer build.
- Confirm kernels actually used (avoid accidental FP16 fallback, or mixed precision changing across prompts).
- Check for long-context only failures → likely attention scaling / alignment / KV cache issues.
- Check for code/JSON-only failures → look for NaN/Inf propagation or formatting instability.
- Compare FP8 vs INT8: if only INT8 fails, likely dequant/fuse path or calibration/scales.

Model-family notes (quick)
These are intentionally high-level; the compatibility doc has per-layer caveats.
- Llama-family (chat): typically stable under FP8 when attention scaling is correct; long-context retrieval is the canary. INT8 can show more code/JSON brittleness if conversion overhead changes timing (watch tool calling prompts).
- Qwen-family: multilingual prompts are more sensitive; watch CJK + punctuation-heavy JSON.
- Mistral-family: code and formatting prompts tend to be strong indicators; also watch summarization-with-quotes.

Known issues / reminders from sprint so far
- If you see “intermittent” quality failures on a specific GPU SKU, treat as correctness until proven otherwise (don’t assume it’s randomness). We had at least one L40S-specific fused-op issue that looked like flakiness at first (see runtime hotfix notes).
- Customer-reported “FP8 output quality intermittent” (SUP-6194) aligns with this: we should reproduce with our watchlist prompts + their rough prompt category (they mentioned long doc + extraction).

What should block shipping vs what can be documented
Block (hard):
- Any deterministic drift Red threshold on the core prompt set
- JSON/function call parse validity < 99% on the JSON subset
- Any NaN/Inf / obviously corrupted output
- Refusal behavior flips on internal safety subset beyond the small tolerance

Document / mitigate (soft):
- Small deterministic drift (Yellow) but no behavior regressions; acceptable behind a non-default flag / allowlist
- Sampling-mode differences without repetition/format issues

Open questions / TODO
- Do we want per-model thresholds? (Probably yes for multilingual-heavy models; but keep global defaults for CI gating.)
- Add explicit “KV cache stress” prompts: same question repeated with growing context to catch decode-loop drift.
- Decide final gating metric for ENG-24819: token agreement vs divergence index vs JSON validity. My vote: JSON validity is a hard gate; token agreement/divergence index as warning gate unless very low.
- Need a stable prompt set versioning scheme + storage location that benchmark-lab can fetch (Rina coordinating).

Notes to self
- Keep the sanity evals small enough that kernel engineers will actually run them during profiling iterations.
- When in doubt: prioritize structured output / tool calls + long-context retrieval. Those are the most customer-visible regressions.
